summary: Fourteen small arcades on two levels, divided by spiral-fluted columns, frame a sequence of biblical scenes on this mid-fourth-century sarcophagus. In the lower register, at the far left, Christ (now headless) stands before the swathed figure of Lazarus in his tomb, and further along a woman kneels at the feet of a figure in a toga, a familiar shorthand for Christ's healing miracles; a veiled orant, the praying soul of the deceased, stands at the centre. On the right short side, carved in continuous relief, the Magi bring their gifts to the Virgin and Child and Christ rides into Jerusalem on a donkey.
facts: According to the Commons description by Jean-Pol Grandmont, the sarcophagus came from the church of Saint-Honorat des Alyscamps, served as the high altar until the 18th century and then as a baptismal font in Saint-Trophime.

The French Wikipedia article on the sarcophagi of Arles singles it out as a composition that breaks with the continuous friezes of earlier work: two superposed registers subdivided by columns and arcades, datable to the mid-4th century.
It is a classified historic monument (Palissy PM13000293).
notes: Many heads are lost, so several scenes are identified only from their composition (Lazarus at lower left; the kneeling woman, probably the woman with an issue of blood). The Magi and the Entry into Jerusalem are on the right short side, visible in other photographs in the Commons category.

summary: Five arcades on spiral-fluted columns frame scenes of Christ's ministry around a damaged central niche, where two soldiers once kept watch beneath a jewelled cross. To the left Christ lays his hand on the eyes of a small blind man; to the right he foretells Peter's denial, the cockerel at their feet; at either end he heals a small male and a kneeling female petitioner. The lid adds Christ giving the keys to Peter, a raising of the dead and the multiplication of the loaves, flanking a blank panel held by winged genii.
facts: Medieval tradition held that it received the remains of Saint Sidonius; the scene of the healing of the blind man was linked with him and gave the tomb its name.

Father Lacordaire later told how monks, fearing Saracen raids around 710, swapped the bodies of Mary Magdalene and Sidonius between their sarcophagi to protect the saint's relics; the story is a legend, not documented history.
The crypt's four sarcophagi are dated to about the end of the 4th century, and several were probably carved in Arles from imported marble.
notes: The two miracles at the ends are not securely identified (proposals include the centurion's servant, the Canaanite woman, or the woman with an issue of blood).

set.original_title: Sarcophage du massacre des saints Innocents (dit de saint Maximin)

summary: At the centre, between palm trees, a bearded Christ stands on the mountain of Paradise from which the four rivers flow, the Lamb at his side; he hands a book to Peter, who bows and carries a cross, and stretches his other hand to Paul. Around them Christ foretells Peter's denial (the cockerel perched between them) and gives him the keys, while Moses receives the Law and Abraham prepares to sacrifice Isaac at the ends. On the lid the shepherds adore the Christ Child warmed by the ox and ass, opposite Herod ordering the massacre of the Innocents.
facts: Long called the sarcophagus of Saint Maximin, it is now named after the Massacre of the Innocents on its lid; French Wikipedia describes the old name as mistaken.
The central Christ is bearded, unlike the youthful, beardless Christ of the miracle scenes, marking him as the exalted Lord giving the Law.
It is one of four late-4th-century sarcophagi in the crypt, which tradition associates with the burial of Mary Magdalene and her companions.

summary: Very worn and mutilated, this columnar sarcophagus belongs to the type of the 'passion sarcophagi'. To the right of the central niche, which probably held a jewelled cross, Christ stands between two guards, raising his hand as he speaks, and in the next niche Pilate sits in judgement, his hand at his chin in doubt. At the left end Paul is led to martyrdom by an executioner drawing his sword; the next scene, an arrest between two soldiers, may show Peter or Paul.
facts: This is the sarcophagus venerated since the late 13th century as the tomb of Mary Magdalene, after Charles II of Anjou had the crypt searched in 1279.
According to French Wikipedia, its short sides show Judas's betrayal and Christ preaching, but they are hard to see in the present display.
The tomb now stands at the back of the crypt and serves as an altar.
notes: Because of the heavy damage, the scenes are identified from the published description rather than from clear details in the photograph.

summary: Between two fields of wavy strigils, a youthful, beardless Christ with long curling hair lays his hand familiarly on the shoulder of a companion, perhaps the deceased welcomed into heaven. At the corners Peter, bearded, and Paul, bald and holding a scroll, turn towards the central pair with gestures of witness or acclamation. The lid shows tritons and dolphins around a blank panel, motifs inherited from Roman marine sarcophagi.
facts: Some authors have identified Christ's companion as Bishop Maximin, the legendary first bishop of Aix.
The lid's tritons and dolphins eating small fish are a decorative survival from pagan marine sarcophagi.
notes: Commons classes it in both the 4th- and 5th-century sarcophagi of France; the identification of the companion is uncertain.

summary: In a single crowded frieze before a backdrop of arcades, Christ stands at the centre with his right hand raised, while to his left Peter shoulders a long cross; two small figures kneel at their feet. The apostles approach from both sides in procession, each raising a hand in acclamation of their Lord. The lid carries a frieze of small winged figures around a central wreath.
facts: Tradition holds that the sarcophagus received the body of Saint Mitrius (Mitre), the martyr venerated in Aix; the Commons description dates it to the end of the 4th century.
It is the most notable piece in the lapidary collection kept in the chapel that forms the narthex of the cathedral's baptistery.
notes: The scene is described from the photograph; the composition with Peter carrying the cross belongs to the family of 'Traditio Legis' sarcophagi.

summary: Carved in a yellowish stone, the frieze unfolds in three groups. At the left, the hand of God stays Abraham's knife as he holds Isaac; in the centre a bearded Christ stands on the mountain of Paradise between palm trees, handing a scroll to Peter while Paul acclaims him; at the right a youthful, long-haired Christ touches the eyes of a blind man with his finger. The gable-roofed lid imitates the tiles of a house, a home for the dead.
facts: It was found in 1970 during work to strengthen a pillar of the nave and had never been opened.
The burial was a woman of about twenty, dressed in silk with gold-thread bands, wearing a crown of plants and a gold cross on her forehead, and laid with incense.
Analysis of the skeleton showed after-effects of poliomyelitis in the right leg.
notes: Robert Valette's Commons description dates it to the mid-5th century.

set.original_title: Sarcophage des compagnons de saint Maurice

summary: Five compartments framed by spiral columns tell a story that moves from teaching to suffering. At the centre Christ, seated, teaches between Peter and Paul, which gave the tomb its other name, 'of Christ the Teacher'. To the right Christ is arrested and brought before Pilate, who sits with his chin in his hand as a servant brings the ewer for washing his hands; to the left Christ appears to Paul, followed by Paul's stoning at Lystra.
facts: The sarcophagi of Saint-Victor were displayed in the Château Borély museum until 1968, when Marseille's mayor Gaston Defferre had them returned to the abbey crypts.
French Wikipedia calls Saint-Victor the most important museum of first-millennium Christian art in Provence after Arles.
notes: Scene identifications follow French Wikipedia; the left-hand scenes are worn.

set.original_title: Sarcophage des compagnes de sainte Ursule

summary: Under seven arches, Christ stands at the centre on a mountain from which four rivers flow, crowned by the hand of God, between Peter carrying a cross and Paul; five apostles stand on each side. On the lid two deer drink between trees, an image of Paradise, while two angels hold a panel beneath a Christogram between dolphins; at the right appear the miracle at Cana and the spies carrying the grape cluster from the Promised Land.
facts: The four rivers of Paradise flowing from Christ's mountain recall the rivers of Eden in Genesis 2:10–14, a common Early Christian image of salvation.
The pairing of Cana with the grape cluster of the Promised Land on the lid juxtaposes a New Testament miracle with its Old Testament foreshadowing.

summary: At the centre of this low relief, Christ sits enthroned within a circular medallion borne by two winged genii, an open book in his hand. At the ends Paul, at the left, and Peter, carrying a cross, turn towards him in acclamation. The flat, linear carving in local stone shows the transformation of Roman funerary sculpture in fifth-century Provence.
facts: Only fragments survive; the sarcophagus was reconstituted with the help of old drawings.
The medallion carried by winged figures adapts the imago clipeata, the shield-portrait of the deceased on Roman sarcophagi, to the figure of Christ.
notes: Parts of the relief are restorations based on drawings.

set.original_title: Sarcophage des brebis et des cerfs

summary: At the centre of the chest the Lamb of God stands on the mountain of Paradise, from which the four rivers flow between palm trees, an image of Christ the sacrificed and victorious Lamb. To the left and right, in more damaged reliefs, Christ performs the miracles of Cana, with its tall water jars, and the multiplication of the loaves. On the lid two flocks of three sheep approach a central Christogram with Alpha and omega.
facts: Like the Christ Enthroned sarcophagus beside it, it was reconstituted with the help of old drawings by Louis Antoine de Ruffi and Joseph Marchand.
French Wikipedia notes a Latinised rho in the Christogram on the lid, flanked by a capital Alpha and a lower-case omega.
notes: Christ appears both symbolically as the Lamb and, in damaged form, in the two miracle scenes.

set.original_title: Cuve de sarcophage dite « tombeau de saint Clair »

summary: A dense crowd of figures fills this continuous frieze. At the left Christ points his rod towards Lazarus, standing swathed in the doorway of a little temple-tomb, while a woman crouches at his feet; in the centre figures holding loaves and baskets on the ground recall the multiplication of the loaves. At the right Abraham grasps the kneeling Isaac, about to sacrifice him, the ram beside the altar.
facts: The sarcophagus was discovered at Auch and is traditionally called the tomb of Saint Clarus.
Wikidata, following the museum's records, lists among its subjects the raising of Lazarus, the feeding of the multitude, the sacrifice of Isaac, Daniel and Adam and Eve.
The photograph is one of the high-resolution images of the Musée Saint-Raymond's collections released under a free licence.
notes: Not every subject listed by Wikidata could be confirmed in the photograph.

summary: Trees with interlacing branches divide this sarcophagus into compartments in which biblical figures stand out in high relief. A veiled orant, the praying soul of the deceased, stands at the centre; around her, figures in tunics and togas carry out a series of miracles, including a youthful figure laying his hand on a small child and another pointing his rod, the usual attributes of Christ the wonder-worker. At the right Daniel stands naked between his lions.
facts: The museum label recorded on Commons states that it was found in Narbonne, on the Boulevard de 1848.
Tree sarcophagi, in which trees replace columns as dividers, are a characteristic Western type of the second half of the 4th century; the Louvre and Arles each hold another.
notes: The individual miracle scenes are not identified in the sources consulted; Christ's presence is inferred from the standard iconography (wonder-worker's rod, healing gesture).

summary: Between two broad fields of wavy strigils, a small central panel shows the Good Shepherd standing between two trees, his sheep at his feet. Worn and flattened, the relief still conveys the gentle simplicity of the image that, more than any other, expressed the Early Christian hope of being carried home by Christ.
facts: The museum label recorded on Commons attributes it to a Narbonne workshop and records its discovery on the Avenue de l'Hérault in Narbonne.

summary: A long, unbroken procession of figures in togas and short tunics fills this fragment, without trees or columns to separate the scenes. At the left a figure sits in a basket-weave chair, the type used for the Virgin receiving the Magi, approached by men in short tunics; towards the right a youthful figure stretches his hand over a basket held out to him, as Christ blesses the loaves, while a veiled woman stands near the centre.
facts: The museum label recorded on Commons notes that it was reused in the walls of the Stadieu house in Narbonne, and that its continuous frieze is unusual for the period.
notes: The scenes are not identified in the sources consulted; the Magi and the multiplication of the loaves are proposed from the composition and are uncertain.

summary: Seven niches crowned by alternating pediments and arches, separated by spiral columns, frame biblical scenes on this Arles-made sarcophagus found in the Ardèche. Christ raises Lazarus, heals the paralytic and a blind man and foretells Peter's denial, while at one end Job sits in conversation with his friends. The photograph shows it in 2022, when it was lent to the Lyon Biennale of contemporary art.
facts: It was discovered in the 16th century at Les Salles, in the commune of Balazuc (Ardèche), and long kept in the church of Saint-Maurice-d'Ardèche.
In 1851 it went to the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Lyon and later to the Gallo-Roman museum at Fourvière (now Lugdunum); a cast is shown in Balazuc town hall.
The scenes were identified by the abbé Joseph-Alexandre Martigny in a memoir published in 1864.

summary: Atlantes support the corners of this crowded frieze, carved in Rome around 330. From left to right Christ heals the woman with an issue of blood, an orant stands between two companions, the soul of the deceased is received by the hand of God (the 'receptio animae' that gives the sarcophagus its name), Christ restores sight to a blind man, and at Cana he touches the water jars with his staff to change water into wine. Its crisp, deeply drilled carving recalls the Roman workshops of the age of Constantine.
facts: Spanish Wikipedia links its workshop stylistically to the sculptors who worked on the Arch of Constantine in Rome.
It comes from the Early Christian necropolis of Zaragoza on this very site and holds relics venerated as those of the 'Santas Masas', the martyrs of Zaragoza.
It was restored in 1998; it is also known as the 'sarcophagus of the Assumption'.

summary: The left part of this frieze is given to three scenes of Peter: the miracle of the spring, his arrest, and Christ foretelling his denial as the cockerel stands by. A praying woman, the orant, occupies the centre; to the right Christ heals a blind man, changes water into wine at Cana, multiplies the loaves and fishes and, at the far end, raises Lazarus from his tomb.
facts: The three Peter scenes on the left gave the sarcophagus its modern name, the 'Petrine trilogy'.
Spanish Wikipedia attributes it to the Roman workshop that produced the Sarcophagus of the Two Brothers in the Vatican.
Only the front is carved; it was restored in 1991.

summary: Biblical episodes crowd one another along this early fourth-century frieze. At the far left Christ raises the swathed Lazarus from a little temple-tomb while a woman kneels at his feet; next, Abraham raises his sword over the kneeling Isaac, and Christ stands among apostles with baskets of loaves at their feet. Adam and Eve stand naked beside a figure who gives them their tasks after the Fall, and at the right three Magi in Phrygian caps bring their gifts to the Christ Child on his mother's lap, seated in a wicker chair.
facts: The sarcophagus was found in 1627 at Layos, in the province of Toledo.
Spanish Wikipedia describes its programme as centred on the dogma of the Incarnation; a replica was displayed in 2007 in the Museo de los Concilios y de la Cultura Visigoda in Toledo.
The photograph was released under a free licence by the Museu Frederic Marès.
notes: Scene identifications are based on the photograph and the subjects listed in the Commons categories of the replica (Lazarus, sacrifice of Isaac, feeding of the multitude, Adam and Eve, Adoration of the Magi).

summary: Seven niches under alternating pediments and arches, divided by spiral-fluted columns, each frame a miracle of Christ, who appears young and beardless with a scroll or a wonder-worker's rod. From left to right he raises the widow's son at Nain, heals a blind man, is touched by the woman with an issue of blood, foretells Peter's denial beside the cockerel, heals the paralytic seated on his couch, multiplies the loaves and fishes, and changes water into wine at Cana. Tritons blowing conches fill the outer spandrels; the fragmentary lid shows the Hebrews in the furnace and Jonah's sea monsters.
facts: It was discovered in 1896 during the rebuilding of the old Molino del Rey in Martos (Jaén); a 1923 report records a tall skeleton and several small pottery jars inside.
It was donated to the Museo de Jaén in 1975; Spanish Wikipedia considers it Italian work, perhaps made for a bishop of ancient Tucci (Martos).
Only about a third of the lid survives.

summary: Three scenes are carved in flat, linear relief across the front, each with a small label panel above. At the centre the Good Shepherd carries a sheep on his shoulders among his flock; to the left is the sacrifice of Isaac by Abraham; to the right Daniel stands with raised arms between the lions. Each image speaks of deliverance, and together they point to Christ, who lays down his life for his sheep.
facts: It was found empty in 1885, five or six metres down, while foundations were dug for a chapel against the north wall of the church; it measures 2.17 m long.
Tradition attributes it to the bishop and martyr Saint Crispin; the Commons description notes Greek inscriptions suggesting a workshop with Byzantine connections in Écija.
Only the front face is decorated, and the lid is missing.

summary: Seven niches framed by spiral columns hold biblical scenes on this fourth-century sarcophagus, now the high altar of the cathedral. Between Old Testament scenes at either end (Abraham's sacrifice and Daniel destroying the dragon), the five central niches show Christ foretelling Peter's denial, healing the paralytic, giving the keys to Peter, healing the woman with an issue of blood and changing water into wine at Cana.
facts: Italian Wikipedia identifies the seven scenes and describes the sarcophagus as one of the most valuable works in the cathedral.
Daniel destroying the dragon (from the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel) is a rarer subject than Daniel among the lions.
notes: Commons dates it '3rd–4th century'; the columnar type with these scenes belongs to the mid- to late 4th century.

set.original_title: Sarcòfag de fris continuat 3 o de Sant Feliu

summary: Eight scenes follow one another without a break across this Constantinian frieze. Peter strikes water from the rock and is arrested by two soldiers; then Christ heals the paralytic, who walks away with his bed, foretells Peter's denial beside the cockerel, changes water into wine at Cana, opens the eyes of a blind man and multiplies the loaves and fishes. At the end Lazarus's tomb stands open while Martha gives thanks.
facts: Popularly called the sarcophagus of Saint Felix, it was long believed to hold the martyr's relics; in 1801 a silver reliquary bust of the saint was placed inside it on the high altar.
After damage in 1936, which also destroyed the silver bust, it was set into the presbytery wall in 1943 alongside the seven other Roman sarcophagi of the church.
The ensemble of eight sarcophagi is considered the most important of its kind preserved in the Iberian Peninsula.

links.label: Conjunt de sarcòfags romans de Sant Feliu de Girona (Catalan Wikipedia)

summary: Seven scenes run in a single line across this frieze, set high in the presbytery wall. Soldiers lead Peter away under arrest; Christ heals the paralytic, changes water into wine beside three jars at Cana, and, at the centre, stretches his hands over two baskets of bread held by apostles, with more baskets at their feet. To the right he opens a blind man's eyes and foretells Peter's denial over the cockerel, and at the end Peter strikes water from the rock for kneeling soldiers to drink.
facts: It repeats seven of the eight scenes of the neighbouring 'sarcophagus of Saint Felix' in a different order, suggesting the same workshop or model.
Catalan Wikipedia notes that some scholars regard it as a local copy of a model from Rome rather than a Roman import.

links.label: Conjunt de sarcòfags romans de Sant Feliu de Girona (Catalan Wikipedia)

notes: Identified with 'continuous frieze 4' by matching the scene order visible in the photograph with the Catalan Wikipedia description.

summary: Two fields of wavy strigils separate three small figures: at the centre a tiny orant prays in an almond-shaped frame, and at each end a shepherd carries a lamb on his shoulders and holds a milk pail. The left-hand shepherd is bearded and older, with a dog at his feet. The orant represents the soul of the deceased in prayer, while the Good Shepherd is an image of Christ who cares for his sheep.
facts: Catalan Wikipedia considers it the oldest Christian strigilated sarcophagus in the Iberian Peninsula, from about 310.
It measures 1.90 m long and 0.61 m high.

links.label: Conjunt de sarcòfags romans de Sant Feliu de Girona (Catalan Wikipedia)

notes: Shepherd figures of this kind can be ambiguous between Christian and pastoral meanings; in this Christian context they are read as the Good Shepherd.

summary: Three carved groups punctuate the strigils. At the centre an orant, probably the deceased, stands between two beardless men, perhaps apostles; at the left two soldiers seize Peter by the arms. At the right Christ, holding a scroll in his left hand, heals a blind man, with a bearded apostle shown at smaller scale.
facts: Catalan Wikipedia notes that Christ, though his face is worn, has short curly hair, matching the 'hero Christ' type of the early 4th century.
It has been suggested that the central orant was originally female and was later reworked as a man with a rudimentary beard.

links.label: Conjunt de sarcòfags romans de Sant Feliu de Girona (Catalan Wikipedia)

summary: At the centre of the front, a youthful Christ sits on a cushioned throne and hands a scroll to Paul, who receives it with veiled hands; from the other side Peter approaches bearing a long cross. The other apostles advance from both ends carrying wreaths of victory in covered hands, a court ceremony transformed into the homage of heaven. Three large monogram crosses decorate the rounded lid, typical of the sarcophagi of Ravenna.
facts: Commons and Sailko's photograph place it among the 5th-century Ravennate sarcophagi lining the aisles of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, which became the burial church of Ravenna's archbishops.
Italian Wikipedia notes that the sarcophagi in Classe, dating from the 5th to the 8th century, allow one to follow the shift from figured reliefs to ever more abstract Byzantine symbols.
The offering of crowns by the apostles adapts the Roman aurum coronarium, the gold wreaths presented to an emperor.

links.label: Basilica di Sant'Apollinare in Classe (Italian Wikipedia)

notes: The name 'of the Twelve Apostles' reflects the apostles distributed over the whole chest; the front shows Christ with six of them.

summary: Eight columns divide the front into five niches: vases sprouting plants fill the outer ones, while in the three central niches Christ stands blessing with an open book, between Paul holding a book and Peter carrying the cross. The rigid, frontal figures speak of the solemn court art of late fifth-century Ravenna. On the lid a wreath encloses the monogram of Christ with alpha and omega between two crosses.
facts: It came from the old church of San Lorenzo in Cesarea, between Ravenna and Classe, and in 1658 received the relics of Saint Barbatian, traditionally the confessor of Galla Placidia.
Its back, only roughly carved, shows two lambs facing the Christogram; each short side has a three-legged candlestick.
Italian Wikipedia compares the stiffness of its figures with those of the sarcophagus of Saint Exuperantius in the same cathedral.

summary: Between two spiral columns and two palm trees heavy with dates, Christ stands at the centre blessing, flanked by Paul with a book on the left and Peter shouldering the cross on the right. The three figures, set against an empty ground, raise their hands in the gestures of speech and acclamation. An inscription runs along the base below them.
facts: Italian Wikipedia dates it to the second decade of the 5th century; it holds the remains of the Ravenna bishop Exuperantius and, since 1809, those of Archbishop Maximian.
The short sides bear a cross and the monogram of Christ, which appears again on the back between two peacocks and two cypresses.
The sarcophagus now serves as the altar table of a chapel set up in 1701.
notes: The inscription on the base is not transcribed here.

set.original_title: Frammento di sarcofago con incredulità di san Tommaso

summary: Two figures stand between palm trees on this sarcophagus fragment. At the left the risen Christ, his head framed by a nimbus, lifts his right arm and draws aside his mantle; Thomas, bearded and wrapped in a heavy pallium, reaches out his finger towards the wound in his side. The quiet encounter captures the moment of doubt turning to faith.
facts: The Incredulity of Thomas is rare on Early Christian sarcophagi; it also appears among the Christological mosaics of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna.
The photograph's title, from the museum display, gives a broad date range of about 390–510.
notes: Only the date range given on Commons is available; the precise date and provenance were not verified.

summary: In a shallow, worn relief on the front, the Lamb of God, its head encircled by a nimbus, stands on a small mound between other lambs, with palm trees at each end. The image of Christ as the sacrificed and victorious Lamb, surrounded by his flock, sums up the hope of the dead in a few quiet forms. Chi-Rho monograms mark the acroteria of the lid.
facts: Tradition associates the sarcophagi in the mausoleum with Galla Placidia, her husband Constantius III and her brother Honorius, but Italian Wikipedia notes that this rests on oral tradition recorded by Agnellus, and Galla Placidia probably died and was buried in Rome in 450.
The mausoleum's three marble sarcophagi stand at the ends of its arms; Commons dates this one to the late 5th or early 6th century.
notes: Christ is represented symbolically, as the nimbed Lamb.

summary: Seven niches divided by columns hold standing figures, and at the centre Christ sits enthroned among them, flanked by a personification of the Church and the apostles. On the lid, small Old Testament scenes, including Noah's ark and Jonah, speak of death and rebirth around a central inscription panel. Reused as the altar of the Renaissance oratory, it now holds the remains of Blessed Giles, companion of Saint Francis.
facts: Italian Wikipedia attributes it to the same workshop as the famous sarcophagus of Junius Bassus in the Vatican Grottoes.
It was previously kept in the crypt of the neighbouring church of San Francesco al Prato.
notes: The photographer's Commons description reads the central scene as Christ the Teacher or a form of the Traditio Legis.

summary: Trees with spreading crowns divide the front of this marble sarcophagus into a sequence of biblical episodes, carved with lively detail down to the dogs at the figures' feet. Near the centre a bearded Christ, raised above the others, hands an unrolled scroll to an apostle who bows to receive it, while another apostle stands on the other side, the composition that the Lamta museum describes as Christ between Peter and Paul. The lid carries hunting scenes on either side of a blank inscription panel.
facts: It was discovered west of Sayada, in the El Karaïa quarter, and is displayed with its carved marble lid in the archaeological museum of Lamta (ancient Leptiminus).
French Wikipedia describes the lid and chest as showing Christ surrounded by the apostles Paul and Peter.
notes: French Wikipedia calls it 'Byzantine', but the tree-sarcophagus type is characteristic of the later 4th century; the date and most side scenes were not verified.

summary: On this small sarcophagus for a child, the story of Jonah fills the front: sailors cast the prophet from a ship under full sail into the coils of the sea monster, while a wind-god blows from above, and at the right Jonah is cast up again amid a tangle of vegetation. At the left end stands a shepherd in a short tunic with a sheep on his shoulders, the Good Shepherd, a sign that the child is carried safely home by Christ.
facts: Jonah, swallowed and released after three days, was read by Early Christians as a sign of Christ's resurrection (Matthew 12:40), and was one of the most popular subjects of pre-Constantinian funerary art.
The museum label photographed on Commons dates it to around AD 300 and gives its origin as Rome.
notes: The inventory number IN 857 comes from the file name of Marie-Lan Nguyen's detail photograph; it was not checked against the museum's catalogue.

summary: High on the wall of a burial chamber, three figures stand in a row: at the right a man wearing a wreath of leaves, and beside him a figure who reaches out with a sprouting branch to touch his head, while a third looks on, a bird flying above. The scene has long been read as the crowning of Christ with thorns, which would make it one of the very earliest images of the Passion. Even if its meaning is debated, it is a moving witness to Christians meditating on a suffering, mocked Lord already in the third century. This image is a Leuven University glass slide of Wilpert's 1903 plate.
facts: The chamber is named the 'cubiculum of the Coronatio' after this scene; Italian Wikipedia dates its paintings to the first decades of the 3rd century.
Nearby on the same walls are other New Testament scenes: the raising of Lazarus, Christ and the Samaritan woman at the well, and the woman with an issue of blood.
The photograph is a glass lantern slide from the University of Louvain, labelled 'Couronnement d'épines (?)' after Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (1903), plate 18.
notes: The identification as the Crowning with Thorns is traditional but debated, as the question mark on the slide label shows; the dating on the slide (100–150) is earlier than the modern dating (early 3rd century).

summary: Above the pool of an underground baptistery, Christ stands in the waters of the Jordan as John the Baptist lays his hand on his head and the dove of the Holy Spirit descends; an angel waits at the side and a deer drinks from the stream. Below, a jewelled cross rises from the water with flowers sprouting from it, so that the newly baptised went down into the font beneath the images of Christ's baptism and of the life-giving cross.
facts: Italian Wikipedia calls this 'submerged baptistery', discovered by Antonio Bosio and fed by natural water, unique among the underground cemeteries of Rome; it dates from the 6th–7th century.
The room was originally a funerary chapel whose plaster covers earlier loculi, transformed into a baptistery in memory of the martyrs Abdon and Sennen.
The image is a University of Louvain glass slide reproducing Wilpert's plates of the cross and the baptism.
notes: The slide reproduces two plates (cross above, baptism below); details are described from Italian Wikipedia as well as the image.

summary: The wall around this arched tomb niche is painted with a small cycle of salvation. Above the arch the three Magi bring their gifts to the Virgin seated with the Child, while to the left Christ, holding his rod, raises Lazarus; the slide label also names Moses striking the rock and the healing of the paralytic, who appears below at the left carrying his bed. Christ's birth, his miracles and the water from the rock together speak of the life promised to the one buried here.
facts: The slide label reads 'Vierge et 3 mages, Lazare, Moïse et rocher, paralytique (IV s.)', and the Leuven record cites Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms, plate 238.
The Catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina is one of the largest in Rome, and contains several distinct paintings of the Magi.
notes: Known only from this tinted glass-slide reproduction of Wilpert's plate; the placement of each scene is described from the image and may be imprecise.

summary: With a few quick strokes the painter shows Christ, young and dressed in tunic and pallium, raising his right hand and holding a long rod as he calls Lazarus from the tomb. Lazarus stands in the doorway of a small temple-like tomb, still wrapped in his grave-clothes. In the Chambers of the Sacraments the scene speaks of the resurrection of the body promised to those buried there.
facts: The Chambers of the Sacraments are small cubicula reached by a gallery of the late 2nd century; Italian Wikipedia dates their paintings to the first half of the 3rd century and describes them as alluding to baptism, the Eucharist and the resurrection.
The glass slide is labelled 'Résurrection de Lazare (déb. III s.)... Chambre des Sacrements' and cites Wilpert, plate 46.

summary: In this lunette above a tomb, the Good Shepherd stands at the centre among his sheep, which turn towards figures who make water flow, perhaps Moses striking the rock, so that the flock may drink. The slide's caption calls it the 'Good Shepherd and the outpouring of the waters of grace': Christ the shepherd gathers his flock to the living water of baptism.
facts: The chamber takes its popular name, 'delle Pecorelle' (of the little sheep), from this painting.
The Leuven record dates it to the second half of the 4th century and cites Wilpert, plate 235, while the slide label dates it to the early 4th century.
notes: The centre of the lunette is cut by a later loculus; the side figures are partly obscured and their identification is uncertain.

summary: A great painted circle fills the vault of this chamber. At its centre the Good Shepherd carries a sheep on his shoulders between two more; in the surrounding compartments scenes from the story of Jonah alternate with praying figures, the orants. The design gathers the hope of rescue and resurrection around the figure of Christ the Shepherd.
facts: The Leuven glass-slide record dates the painting to the first half of the 3rd century and cites Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms, plate 61.
It is distinct from the better-known octagonal Good Shepherd vault in the same catacomb.

summary: Two figures in tunic and pallium face each other on a damaged wall, with a large cockerel between them: Christ and Peter at the moment when Christ foretells that before the cock crows Peter will deny him three times. Both raise a hand, one in speech and the other in protest or dismay. The scene, common on sarcophagi, is much rarer in catacomb painting.
facts: The handwritten label on this University of Louvain glass slide reads 'Rome Cyriaque. 350–400. Négation de S. Pierre. Wilpert 242'.
Peter with the cockerel became a standard Christian image in the 4th century, appearing on many Roman sarcophagi.
notes: The Leuven catalogue gives the location only as 'Catacomba (?)'; the attribution to the Catacomb of Cyriaca rests on the slide's handwritten label. Which of the two figures is Christ cannot be determined with certainty from the reproduction.

summary: The curved vault of this arcosolium is filled with a heavenly assembly: Christ sits enthroned at the centre while the twelve apostles sit in two ranks around him on a golden ground. The monogram of Christ (Chi-Rho) appears below, near the tomb itself. Christ is presented as the teacher and judge whose college of apostles promises the deceased a place in his kingdom.
facts: A University of Louvain glass slide of the same painting (Wilpert, plate 193) is labelled 'Christ et apôtres' and dated around 350–356.
It is a different painting from the smaller lunette in Domitilla showing the seated Christ teaching among his disciples.
notes: Dating follows the Leuven slide record (mid-4th century).

summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a jewelled throne with the Christ Child on her lap, both framed by golden haloes; the Child holds a scroll. On either side stand the martyrs Felix and Adauctus, buried in this catacomb, and the saint at the left lays his hand on the shoulder of Turtura, the widow in dark clothes holding a scroll, presenting her to the Mother of God and her Son. An epitaph below, set up by her son, commemorates her.
facts: English Wikipedia describes the 'tomb of Turtura' as built for a woman by her son, with a fresco of her, the two martyrs and the Madonna and Christ Child; the Commons record dates it to 528.
It stands near the small underground basilica of Felix and Adauctus, re-excavated under Pope John I (523–526) for the martyrs' cult.
notes: Which martyr stands on which side is not stated in the sources consulted.

summary: A young shepherd with a round, boyish face and thick hair stands on a small integral base, carrying a sheep across his shoulders and holding its legs with his right hand; two more animals stand at his feet. He wears a short belted tunic and boots, the working dress of a herdsman. Small statuettes like this one, found across the Mediterranean, made the image of Christ the Good Shepherd present in homes and burial places.
facts: According to the museum label recorded on Commons, it comes from Corinth, dates to the 4th century and has the accession number BXM 2.
The Good Shepherd statuette type is also known from Rome, notably the marble figure in the Museo Pio Cristiano of the Vatican Museums.
notes: As with all such figures, the shepherd type was shared with pagan art; its Christian meaning is inferred from date and context.

summary: From the base of a broken glass bowl, a bust in gold leaf looks out from within two interlaced squares: a youthful figure with curling hair, wearing a tunic and a mantle fastened by a round brooch, with the letters CRIS beside his head. In the corner spaces four small busts surround him. The name identifies the figure as Christ, shown not in a narrative scene but as a portrait at the centre of the vessel.
facts: Gold glasses of this kind, made by sandwiching engraved gold leaf between layers of glass, are mostly known from the catacombs of Rome, where the bases of cups were pressed into the mortar sealing graves.
The number E.C.630 is painted on the fragment, as visible in the photograph.
notes: The British Museum catalogue entry was not consulted; date and provenance follow the general type. Only the letters CRIS are clearly legible.

summary: A husband in a richly folded toga and a wife wearing a jewelled necklace are shown side by side in this cracked gold-glass medallion. Between and above them stands a small figure of Christ, who holds a wreath over each of their heads, blessing their marriage, while an inscription runs around the border. Such glasses were probably wedding gifts, and many were later set into the walls of graves in the catacombs.
facts: Married couples crowned by a small figure of Christ are a recurrent Christian adaptation of the Roman marriage portrait on 4th-century gold glass; another example is in the Bargello, Florence.
Commons classes it among gold-glass portraits showing the toga contabulata, the folded toga of the later Roman Empire.
notes: The inscription is only partly legible and is not transcribed; the British Museum's registration details were not verified.
